senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: positive moral qualities of the most general nature
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no abstract term such as ‘goodness.’ Since goodness implies some type of activity involving others, one must frequently use a verb expression, for example, ‘to be good to’ or ‘to benefit.’ The qualification ‘full of’ in Romans 15:14 must likewise be restructured in a number of languages so as to indicate the fact that one always engages in doing good, for example, ‘that you are always doing good to people.’

senses.def: the act of generous giving, with the implication of its relationship to goodness
the uncertainty of some event or state
pertaining to being shamefully greedy for material gain or profit
pertaining to what cannot be uttered or expressed
glosses: what cannot be expressed in words

senses.def: pertaining to not being readily shaken in one’s opinions or beliefs
to get rid of someone by execution, often with legal or quasi-legal procedures
to remove or withdraw the validation of something
to formally and legally declare that someone who is not one’s own child is henceforth to be treated and cared for as one’s own child, including complete rights of inheritance
senses.comment: In a number of languages adoption is spoken of as ‘making a child a son’ or ‘causing a child to become a daughter.’ In some instances the equivalent expression is merely ‘to treat someone as a son’ or ‘… daughter.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀνάχυσις ‘flood,’ not occurring in the NT) an extremely high point on a scale of extent and implying an excess of something with negative value
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of this phrase in 1 Peter 4:4 is ‘they lived very bad lives’ or ‘there was nothing bad that they didn’t do.’

senses.def: to complete something by adding what is still lacking
pertaining to that which does not change from one state to another
the process of dying
senses.comment: In a number of languages clear distinctions are made in the use of terms for dying on the basis of the manner or circumstances of death. For example, one term may refer to death primarily as the result of old age, while another term may refer to death caused by sickness, and still other terms may be used for death caused by violence. Careful distinctions must be used in determining the choice of terms based on particular contexts.|In John 6:50 ἀποθνῄσκω must be understood in a spiritual rather than in a strictly literal sense. This bold figurative language is characteristic of the Gospel of John and should not be eliminated, though in some languages a strictly literal translation may be understood only in a literal sense and thus lead to misinterpretation. In some instances, therefore, it may be necessary to suggest the metaphorical significance by translating ‘he will not, as it were, die.’

senses.def: to be in imminent danger of dying
senses.comment: It would also be possible to render καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἀποθνῄσκω in 1 Corinthians 15:31 as ‘I am in danger of being killed each day.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποθνῄσκω[a] ‘to die,’ 23.99) to be unable to respond or react to any impulse or desire
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of ‘dying to sin.’ In some instances one can preserve the figurative meaning by an expression such as ‘to be like dead as far as desiring to sin’ or ‘to be like a corpse as far as temptations to sin are concerned.’

senses.def: purposely to avoid association with someone
glosses: to have nothing to do with

senses.def: to grab or seize by force, with the purpose of removing and/or controlling
senses.comment: In Matthew 13:19 the context as a whole is figurative, but a more or less literal rendering of ‘snatches’ or ‘seizes’ is probably satisfactory.

senses.def: to attack, with the implication of seizing
senses.comment: It is also possible that in Matthew 11:12 ἁρπάζω is to be understood in the sense of ‘attack’: βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν ‘violent men attack it.’

senses.def: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
to gain control over by force
senses.comment: Though in John 10:28 ἁρπάζω would appear to be in a literal context in view of the expression ἐκ τῆς χειρός μου ‘out of my hand,’ nevertheless ἁρπάζω is certainly figurative in meaning and so is χείρ ‘hand.’

senses.def: to be without a permanent residence and thus engaged in travelling from one place to another
glosses: to wander from place to place
to be constantly going from place to place
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in 1 Corinthians 4:11, see 85.80.

senses.def: to not have a place of residence
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in 1 Corinthians 4:11, see ἀστατέω[a] 15.25.

senses.def: to cease to exist, with the implication of no longer being evident or visible
to experience difficulty by burdensome and troublous obligations
(an idiom, literally: to be burdened by sleep) to be in a state of deep sleep
(an idiom, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

senses.def: pertaining to the use of violent or strong force
to cause to go down into water or other liquid substance
(a figurative extension of meaning of βυθίζω[a] ‘to cause to sink,’ 15.115) to cause someone to experience serious consequences

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: the period of advanced age, normally of a person beyond his or her prime
a major OT prophet
a Roman silver coin equivalent to a days wage of a common laborer
senses.comment: The practice of translating terms for coins with specific monetary values has differed widely in different languages at different times and in different contexts. One of the most serious problems has been the recent rapid inflation which has taken place in many parts of the world and which has thus made traditional renderings relatively meaningless or even absurd. For a number of years the silver content in an ancient denarius was equivalent to twenty cents U.S., but the value of silver has changed appreciably within recent times, and therefore any calculation based upon the value of silver content in ancient coins is misleading. Furthermore, in ancient times silver coins had proportionately far more buying power than the equivalent amount of silver would have today. Therefore, a number of translators have attempted in some measure to relate coinage to buying power, or perhaps better, to earning power. For example, in Mark 6:37 the reference to ‘two hundred denarii’ is sometimes translated as ‘the equivalent of 200 days’ wages’ or even ‘eight months of a laborer’s wages.’|In Matthew 18:28 the reference to ‘a hundred denarii’ is designed primarily to indicate the contrast between the enormous sum owed by one servant in contrast with the very small amount owed by the fellow servant. In this instance the contrast may be expressed in terms of ‘thousands of denarii’ in contrast with a ‘few denarii.’ In such a case the equivalent coinage may be turned into a local currency, for example, ‘thousands of dollars’ in contrast with a ‘few dollars.’ In a number of cases translators have attempted to avoid any specific reference to a particular coin and have simply spoken of ‘silver coins’ or ‘gold coins’ without indicating particular values. Under such circumstances a marginal note is sometimes employed in order to indicate the relative value of the currency.

senses.def: to tear or rip in two (as of clothing)
senses.comment: In the NT tearing of clothing was a symbol of horror associated with sacrilege. In many cultures, however, the tearing of clothing may be associated only with insanity. It may therefore be important to add a phrase in describing ‘the tearing of clothing’ in order to mark the significance, for example, ‘to show horror’ (Matthew 26:65, Acts 14:14) and in the OT ‘to show mourning’ (,).

senses.def: to cause someone to be in a proper or right relation with someone else
glosses: to cause to be in a right relationship with
senses.comment: Some scholars, however, interpret δικαιόω, δικαίωσις, and δικαιοσύνη in the contexts of Romans 3:24, Romans 4:25, and Romans 1:17 as meaning forensic righteousness, that is to say, the act of being declared righteous on the basis of Christ’s atoning ministry; but it would seem more probable that Paul uses these expressions in the context of the covenant relation rather than in the context of legal procedures.|It may be difficult in some languages to find a succinct expression equivalent to ‘to be put right with.’ Sometimes the closest equivalent may be ‘to be related to as one should be.’ In some instances the implication of a right relationship may be expressed by phrases involving ‘acceptance.’ For example, Romans 3:24 may be expressed as ‘by the free gift of God’s grace they are accepted by him through Christ Jesus who sets them free.’ Similarly, Romans 4:25 is sometimes expressed as ‘he was raised to life in order to cause us to be accepted by God.’ There are, however, certain dangers involved in terms indicating ‘acceptance,’ since this might imply God’s reluctance to accept people apart from the atoning work of Jesus Christ, while in reality it was God who was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. Therefore, one should clearly avoid a rendering which would seem to suggest different types of motivation in the Godhead.

senses.def: the act of clearing someone of transgression
senses.comment: In a number of languages the process of acquittal takes the form of a direct statement, for example, ‘to say, You are not guilty’ or ‘…, You no longer have sin’ or, as expressed idiomatically in some instances, ‘…, Sin is no longer on your head’ or ‘…, Your sins are now given back to you.’

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry
senses.def: a large, curved knife employed in cutting ripe grain or grapes
senses.comment: Where there is no receptor language term for sickle, one may often employ a descriptive phrase such as ‘a knife for harvesting grain’ or ‘a curved knife for cutting grain.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to throw a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
senses.comment: In Revelation 14:16 and Revelation 14:19 this idiom occurs in a figurative context, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘harvesting’ rather than using a phrase which mentions the literal use of a sickle.

senses.def: (idioms, literally: to send a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
senses.comment: In Revelation 14:15 and Revelation 14:18 this idiom occurs in a figurative context, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘harvesting’ rather than using a phrase which mentions the literal use of a sickle.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to exercise complete control over one’s desires and actions
senses.comment: An adequate rendering of the expression ‘to exercise self-control’ may require an idiomatic equivalent, for example, ‘to hold oneself in,’ ‘to command oneself,’ ‘to be a chief of oneself,’ ‘to make one’s heart be obedient,’ ‘to command one’s own desires,’ ‘to be the master of what one wants,’ or ‘to say No to one’s body.’ (Compare ἀκρασία ‘lack of self-control,’ 88.91, and ἀκρατής ‘lacking in self-control,’ 88.92.)

senses.def: a Roman officer in command of about one hundred men
senses.comment: In a number of languages, centurion can very readily be rendered by a phrase such as ‘a commander of a hundred soldiers,’ but in many instances the closest natural equivalent is simply ‘captain.’

senses.def: to be so amazed as to be practically overwhelmed
a painful, ulcerated sore resulting from infection
(derivative of ἐνδείκνυμαι[a] ‘to show, to demonstrate,’ 28.51) the means by which one knows that something is a fact
to speak against someone in an insolent and arrogant way
the events associated with the celebration of a festival or feast
senses.comment: Though various celebrations of the Jewish religious year have traditionally been called ‘feasts,’ it would be wrong to use a term which would suggest gluttony or wasteful abundance of food. The emphasis should be upon the ceremonial character of the eating rather than upon the extent of what was eaten. Therefore, it may be better in a number of languages to use terms referring to ‘celebrations’ or ‘festivals,’ since the festivities of such gatherings were far more important than the feasting.

senses.def: a brief notice used primarily for identification
one who has the responsibility of caring for spiritual concerns
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 2:25 ἐπίσκοπος is applied to Christ, and it no doubt shares certain of the meanings associated with ἐπίσκοπος[b] in 53.71, but the focus in 1 Peter 2:25 is not upon leadership but upon the role of caring for the believers.

senses.def: one who serves as a leader in a church
senses.comment: For ἐπίσκοπος in 1 Peter 2:25, see 35.43.|In translating ἐπισκοπή[b] (53.69), ἐπισκοπέω[c] (53.70), or ἐπίσκοπος[b], it is important to try to combine the concepts of both service and leadership, in other words, the responsibility of caring for the needs of a congregation as well as directing the activities of the membership. In some translations an equivalent may be ‘helper’ and ‘leader.’

senses.def: to express differences of opinion, with at least some measure of antagonism or hostility

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: to experience an appropriate occasion for some activity
glosses: to have an appropriate time for

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: to spend time in an enjoyable and profitable manner

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a class or division of persons who perform certain daily duties (in the one NT occurrence, a reference to a group of priests performing certain functions in the Temple at Jerusalem)
senses.comment: It may be necessary to expand somewhat the expression ‘the work group of Abijah’ (Luke 1:5) to read ‘a work group known as the division of Abijah.’ Otherwise, one might get the impression that this was a work group under the command of Abijah or a group of persons who belonged specifically to the person named Abijah. If it is difficult to obtain a satisfactory expression for ‘work group,’ one can of course translate the final clause of Luke 1:5 as simply ‘who belonged to a group of priests known as the group of Abijah.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: according to Hebrew reckoning (as reflected in the NT), a period of time beginning at sunset and ending at the following sunset

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: the daylight period between sunrise and sunset (divided into twelve hours)

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: an indefinite unit of time (whether grammatically singular or plural), but not particularly long (note the contrast with αἰών[a] ‘age,’ 67.143, and γενεά[d] ‘age,’ 67.144)
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term such as ‘period’ referring to an indefinite extent of time. One can, however, render Luke 1:23 as ‘when he no longer had to serve in the Temple’ or ‘when he had finished the days when he served in the Temple.’

senses.def: the light of the day in contrast with the darkness of night (see νύξ[b] ‘night,’ 14.59)
senses.comment: In order to focus attention upon the beginning of daylight, one may translate Luke 4:42 as ‘when the sun began to shine’ or ‘when the sky began to become light’ or even ‘when it was no longer night.’|In some languages there is no noun for either ‘day’ or ‘daylight,’ but a verb expression may be employed which may be rendered literally as ‘to day’ or ‘to become day.’

senses.def: a court of justice for determining guilt or innocence
senses.comment: For languages which do not have technical terms for a court, it is usually possible to use some such phrase as ‘to be brought before a judge’ or ‘to have judges decide one’s case.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (idioms, literally: day out of day, and: throughout day, respectively) a relatively long period of time
(an idiom, literally: day of slaughter) a time of destructive judgment
senses.comment: The reference of the phrase ἡμέρᾳ σφαγῆς in James 5:5 is the destructive judgment of God, but it is possible that σφαγῆς should be interpreted in a more literal sense of ‘destruction’ rather than mere condemnation.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (idioms, literally: forty days and forty nights, forty days, respectively) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
senses.comment: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to advance in days) to be quite advanced in age

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (expressions, literally: night and day, day and night, day and day, respectively) duration of time, either continuous or episodic, but without limits
time in an eschatological frame, referring to a final judgment or to the coming of Christ

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: through days) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of a few days
pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

senses.def: to slaughter an animal in a ritual manner as a sacrifice to deity
to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
an emphatic marker of comparison between events and states

large quadruped mammal; Camelus dromedarius and Camelus bactrianus; bactrians may reach 2 m.; dromedaries are bigger and a uniform light fawn color; bactrians are darker; suited to life in desert areas; store excess food in their humps, can go without water for long periods; can make long journeys through dry areas; used for riding and for carrying heavy loads and pulling carts; hair woven into cloth used for making tents or outer robes; milk used as food and drink; symbol of wealth and commerce
senses.comment: In most areas where camels are not known, a term for ‘camel’ has been borrowed from a dominant language. In other instances people may have constructed descriptive phrases. For example, in Timorese the first two expressions suggested for camel were ‘the horse with a crooked back’ or ‘the long-legged horse,’ but finally people settled upon a more satisfactory rendering, namely, ‘the horse of the desert.’ In a number of languages a camel is simply called ‘the big humped animal.’ In a number of cases, however, it may be useful to have some kind of a description of a camel in a glossary or word list.|In referring to the camel’s hair garment worn by John the Baptist, there are two problems. In the first place, it is important to translate the phrase ‘garment of camel’s hair’ in such a way as to indicate that the garment was made of cloth woven out of camel’s hair and did not consist of the entire skin nor of camel’s hair stuck onto John the Baptist’s body. In the second place, it is important to indicate that this camel’s hair garment was a kind of rough garment, since in a number of languages an expression such as ‘camel’s hair coat’ would refer to an expensive, luxury garment. See also 6.216.

senses.def: to judge someone as definitely guilty and thus subject to punishment
glosses: to render a verdict of guilt

senses.def: to experience, with the implication of something having been bestowed upon
senses.comment: In some languages it may be more natural to translate as ‘and wanting the Jews to show him good will’ or ‘and hoping that the Jews would like him.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: a sharp, pointed projection used in stinging

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry
senses.def: a pointed stick used in driving draft animals
senses.comment: In the NT κέντρον[b] occurs only in the idiom πρὸς κέντρον λακτίζειν 'to kick against the goad;' meaning to hurt oneself by active resistance. See 39.19.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of κέντρον[a] ‘sting,’ 8.45) the power or ability to kill or destroy
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κέντρον in 1 Corinthians 15:55, see 24.86.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of κέντρον[a] ‘sting,’ 8.45) the means or capacity to cause severe suffering
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κέντρον in 1 Corinthians 15:55, see 20.69.

senses.def: to urgently invite someone to accept responsibilities for a particular task, implying a new relationship to the one who does the calling
senses.comment: It is rare that one can translate καλέω[d], κλῆσις[a], and προσκαλέω[b] as simply ‘to call’ in the sense of ‘to speak to someone at a distance and tell them to come.’ For example, in 2 Thessalonians 2:14 it may be necessary to render the above clause as ‘through the good news we preached, which summoned you to do this.’ Similarly, in Acts 16:10 one may translate ‘because God has urgently invited us to preach the good news to the people there.’

senses.def: the state of having been called to a particular task and/or relation
senses.comment: As in the case of καλέω[d], κλῆσις[a], and προσκαλέω[b] (33.312), it may be entirely impossible to use a term in a receptor language which means literally ‘to call.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to translate Ephesians 4:1 as ‘I ask you then … live worthy of the responsibility which God has urgently invited you to accept’ or ‘… live worthy of the task which God has given you to do.’

senses.def: the station in life or social role which one has
senses.comment: In this context, κλῆσις refers to the status or role of being either a slave or a free person. In a number of languages this expression in 1 Corinthians 7:20 can be best translated as ‘everyone should continue to be the same kind of person that he was when he was called.’ Such an expression must, of course, refer to one’s position in society and in the total social structure, not to particular aspects of moral or immoral behavior.

senses.def: a Roman centurion to whom Peter ministered
the motion of an object rolling back and forth or rolling about
senses.comment: It is rare that one can use in a language the same or related terms for the rolling of a person in an epileptic fit and the wallowing of a pig in the mud. The first is chaotic and uncontrolled, while the second is both purposeful and slower.

senses.def: to serve, with the implication of more formal or regular service
(derivative of λειτουργέω[a] ‘to serve,’ 35.22) an assignment or role in serving
senses.comment: The meaning of ‘ministry’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘a way of serving.’

senses.def: to perform religious rites as part of one’s religious duties or as the result of one’s role
a projection on the south coast of Asia Minor
to think or reason in a completely irrational manner
glosses: to not be in one’s right mind
to be out of one’s mind
senses.comment: In some languages μανία is best rendered by an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘thoughts that never return,’ ‘distorted thoughts,’ ‘senseless thoughts,’ or ‘thoughts that cannot be understood.’

senses.def: a relatively emphatic marker of contrast
senses.comment: For other interpretations of μενοῦν in Luke 11:28, see 89.50 and 91.8.

senses.def: a marker of result, often implying the conclusion of a process of reasoning
senses.comment: For other interpretations of μενοῦν in Luke 11:28, see 89.128 and 91.8.

senses.def: a marker of considerable emphasis (in comparison with δήπου[b], 91.7)
senses.comment: For other interpretations of μενοῦν in Luke 11:28, see 89.50 and 89.128.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
senses.def: an indefinite negated point of time

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: to be left without a family
senses.comment: In 1 Timothy 5:5 χήρα would mean that the woman’s husband had died, but μεμονωμένη would imply that she had no relatives who would be in a position to help her.

senses.def: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the territory of the tribe of Naphtali
the process of becoming sleepy
senses.comment: ‘To grow drowsy’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to begin to nod’ or ‘their heads fell’ or ‘their eyes gradually closed.’|In 2 Peter 2:3 νυστάζω occurs in a highly figurative context: καὶ ἡ ἀπώλεια αὐτῶν οὐ νυστάζει, literally ‘and their destruction is not drowsy,’ meaning either ‘their destruction is imminent’ or ‘their Destroyer has been wide awake’ (see Today’s English Version).

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend a period of time, with the implication of lack of activity
any type of tool or instrument
senses.comment: In Romans 6:13 ὅπλον is generally interpreted as being used figuratively as a reference to parts of the body which may be instruments for doing evil.

senses.def: an instrument used in fighting, whether offensive or defensive
senses.comment: In the NT ὅπλον[b] also occurs in the figurative sense of non-material means of fighting, e.g. 2 Corinthians 6:7.

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a negative reference to an entity, event, or state
a place for the lodging of travellers
to abandon a former relationship or association, or to dissociate (a type of reversal of beginning to associate)
the Jewish festival commemorating the deliverance of Jews from Egypt
senses.comment: In some languages the term πάσχα has been borrowed in one form or another, but frequently it is necessary to have some qualifying statement to identify this festival, for example, ‘a festival to celebrate the passing over of the angel’ or ‘a festival to celebrate deliverance from Egypt.’

senses.def: a Passover meal eaten in connection with the Passover festival (see 51.6)
a specially selected lamb (or a collective for all such lambs) killed and eaten during the festival commemorating the departure of Israel from Egypt
senses.comment: The term πάσχα (a borrowing from Hebrew) has three different meanings which refer to three different aspects of the Passover. In a context which speaks of ‘the Passover taking place’ (Matthew 26:2), the meaning is the festival (51.6). With a term such as ἑτοιμάζειν ‘to prepare’ (Matthew 26:19), the term πάσχα means ‘the Passover meal,’ that is to say, ‘to prepare the Passover meal’ (51.7). But with a term meaning ‘to kill’ or ‘to sacrifice’ (Luke 22:7), the meaning is ‘the Passover lamb.’ These different meanings in Greek reflect similar uses in Hebrew.|It is often impossible, however, to use a phrase such as ‘Passover lamb,’ since a literal rendering may suggest ‘a lamb that passes over’ or ‘a lamb that someone has passed over,’ either in the sense of ‘ridden over’ or ‘neglected.’ It is therefore necessary in many languages to expand the phrase ‘the Passover lamb’ to read ‘the lamb that is eaten at the Passover Festival’ or ‘the lamb associated with the Festival that celebrates the passing over.’ It may even be necessary to expand the phrase ‘passing over’ to refer specifically to the passing over of the angel of death, and in certain instances one cannot even employ a literal rendering such as ‘passing over,’ since this might mean merely ‘flying above.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to use an expression roughly equivalent to ‘passing by.’ It may, however, be better to use a short, though somewhat obscure, expression in the text and provide a full explanation in a marginal note or glossary.

senses.def: to tie or wrap an object around something
to cause someone to become rich
senses.comment: The causative in πλουτίζω may sometimes be expressed by a verb meaning ‘to help,’ for example, ‘will help you become rich.’

senses.def: to cause someone to have an abundance of that which is of value or worth
glosses: to cause to have an abundance of
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 1:5 the final phrase, ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ πάσω γνώσει, indicates that the abundance refers to both the quantity of messages and the knowledge.

senses.def: liquids used for nourishment or to satisfy thirst
senses.comment: Though in many languages the equivalent of πόσις and πόμα would be a verbal derivative meaning basically ‘that which is drunk,’ in other languages the equivalent may be ‘watery food’ or ‘liquid food.’|In some languages, however, one cannot refer to ‘blood’ (John 6:55) as being ‘drink,’ since blood is classified as food rather than as drink. On the other hand, it may be possible to translate ‘my blood is the real drink’ as ‘my blood is real nourishment.’ The expression ‘food and drink’ (Hebrews 9:10) may be better rendered in some languages as ‘all kinds of food.’

senses.def: consumption of liquids, particularly water and wine
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between drinking water and drinking alcoholic beverages. Still other terms may be employed in speaking of drinking soups or broths.

senses.def: to make ready or prepare in advance

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: the early part of the daylight period

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to violate moral principles by acting in an unscrupulous manner
senses.comment: ῥᾳδιουργία and ῥᾳδιούργημα may often be rendered simply as ‘doing what one should not do.’ These terms also may often be translated merely as ‘cheating.’

senses.def: to cause someone to be or to become more able or capable, with the implication of a contrast with weakness
senses.comment: The terms στηρίζω (see 74.19) and σθενόω in 1 Peter 5:10 are very similar in meaning and serve primarily to intensify the meaning of making persons more able to engage in or to undergo certain experiences.

senses.def: pertaining to being sad and discouraged
groaning or sighing as the result of deep concern or stress
senses.comment: To groan or to sigh may be the result of quite different circumstances, and in a number of languages a clear distinction must be made in any term for groaning or sighing, depending upon the reason or basis for such an expression of emotion. In Mark 7:34 the sigh or groan would seem to be an expression of sympathy for the deaf-mute, but in Acts 7:34 the groans would be caused by severe misery and oppression.

senses.def: to stir up hostility against
to cause to come together, whether of animate or inanimate objects
to be of an advantage to someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages the idea of ‘advantage’ implies some comparison, either a benefit which is greater than someone else has or a benefit which makes one’s later state better off than the previous state. For example, in the case of John 11:50 one may translate ‘don’t you realize that if one man dies for the people, then you are much better off.’

senses.def: to bury someone along with someone else
senses.comment: In Romans 6:4 συνθάπτω is used figuratively, since it evidently had not yet acquired a conventional figurative meaning. In a number of languages it is necessary to mark this figurative usage by means of a simile, for example, ‘we were, so to speak, buried with him.’

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
senses.def: thick cord formed by twisting or braiding several strands together; made of a variety of materials, including palm fibers, linen, or reeds
senses.comment: The ropes mentioned in Acts 27:32 would obviously have been rather thick, while in John 2:15 the whip which Jesus made in driving the animals and merchants out of the Temple would probably have consisted of strong cords.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to make perfect in the moral sense
senses.comment: For another interpretation of τελειόω in 1 John 2:5, see 73.7.

senses.def: to cause to be truly and completely genuine
senses.comment: For another interpretation of τελειόω in 1 John 2:5, see 88.38.

senses.def: to bring an activity to a successful finish
to be completely successful in accomplishing some goal or attaining some state
senses.comment: For another interpretation of τελειόω in Philippians 3:12, see 53.50.

senses.def: to admit into or initiate into faith (possibly based on technical usage in the mystery religions)
senses.comment: It is important that in Philippians 3:12 τελειόω is to be understood in the sense of a functional stage of religious attainment: ‘I have already become an initiate.’ For another interpretation of τελειόω in Philippians 3:12, see 68.31.

senses.def: to cause to happen for some end result
to attain a state as a goal
(comparative adverb of τολμηρός ‘bold, daring,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to an activity involving unusual boldness or daring
a city on the Phoenician coast
to be more abundant than a given quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to indicate the overabundance of grace in 1 Timothy 1:14, since there is nothing in the context to provide a basis for comparison. Accordingly, the closest equivalent may be ‘but the grace of our Lord was very, very much.’

senses.def: to cause something to become high

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: to cause someone to have high status
pertaining to love for God

senses.comment: Some languages make a clear distinction between various kinds of leaves, especially a difference between leaves which have parallel veins and those which have branching veins. In Mark 11:13 what is important is that the fig tree was ‘in leaf,’ that is to say, the leaves had already come out after the winter season. In a number of languages a tree in this state may be referred to as ‘a tree which is green.’

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a basic inner garment worn under the ἱμάτιον[b] ‘cloak’ (6.172)

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any kind of clothing
to provide a false or untrue witness
senses.comment: A person who gives false witness may deceive in two aspects, (1) in pretending to have been an eyewitness to an event and (2) in saying what is not true, but the focal element in ψευδομαρτυρέω is the fact that what is said is not true.
